articles.title: The price of what low-skilled workers know
articles.summary: It is heartening to see Indian workers helping generate the data that will drive the next generation of robots and artificial intelligence. Every month, a fresh batch of images does the rounds on LinkedIn and X: Indian factory employees with cameras strapped to their heads, their every movement recorded to train AI systems. The message? Tasks once thought resistant to automation are suddenly within AI’s reach. But these images of Indian workers wearing cameras should provoke something more serious than technological excitement or dystopian alarm. They should provoke a strategic question: Who owns data? Who builds models? Who controls these machines, and where does the resulting value accumulate?The instinctive reaction, of course, is enthusiasm, and these images are easy to celebrate. Yes, AI training is happening in India, and Indian workers are part of it. Gig, factory, and service workers are capturing ordinary physical tasks from a first-person perspective, and thousands of hours of Indian movement are becoming training material for the next generation of AI. Participation is not however synonymous with power. The important question to ask is not whether artificial intelligence is being trained in India. It’s what India is contributing to the process, on what terms, and who will ultimately own the productive assets created from it.Also read | Your boss may soon know what you’re asking Claude to do at workSeveral reports show that filming factory workers is fast becoming normal across Indian cities. In Gurugram and Nagpur, for example, workers are being recorded as they sew, adjust loom tension, and clear machine jams, or are simply under surveillance as they work. Similar data collection is spreading across the service economy. Human Archive, a Silicon Valley-based physical AI data startup, says it has deployed more than 1,000 headsets through partners in India and pays a base rate of $1 an hour for egocentric data collection, acknowledging that its Indian network helps keep compensation lower. Put simply, India’s cheap labour is becoming cheap machine-training data, too.The ambitions extend far beyond individual experiments and individual startups. EgoLab, an Indian startup which has been collecting first-person footage from Indian factories, was acquired in 2026 by US-registered Build Artificial Intelligence Inc. EgoLab's own material, reviewed by scroll had described their ambition to collect $100 million in footage from 100 million factory workers across major Indian states and sectors, including textiles, automobiles, chemicals, electronics, FMCG, and steel. BuildAI's published current roadmap similarly includes an ego-centric 100-million-dataset target for October 2027.These are not outcomes, but these ambitions reveal the intended scale of how India's data is being converted into a dataset that can be aggregated, transferred, and used globally. A worker wearing a camera records two outputs. The immediate output is the product of labour and information about how that labour is performed. In the future AI economy, the work is just not generating output; it is also recording the work, which can generate capital in the future.Also read | Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu sees a painful rebalancing of jobs in the AI ageThis is very relevant for a country where 88% of the workers are employed in occupations classified as low competency. This classification may make sense within the conventional labour market, but the same task has become extraordinarily valuable from the perspective of physical AI. Large language models could learn from vast stores of digitized text, images, and code; Physical AI there is no equivalent archive for much of what humans know about operating in the real world. Robotic Machines still struggle with actions people perform almost automatically: adjusting grips and pressure, manipulating unfamiliar objects, coordinating hands and tools, recovering from mistakes, and adapting when physical, emotional, and other conditions change. Therefore, what is routine knowledge for a human worker can become frontier knowledge for a machine. India's workforce is not only a source of inexpensive labour; it is also a potentially enormous reservoir for the demonstration that physical AI still needs to learn how the world works. However, a country that built its IT boom on labour-cost arbitrage, in practice, introduces a striking inversion: cheaper labour once reduced the incentive to automate. Now, if human demonstration can also be acquired cheaply, low wages may also help reduce the cost of teaching automation itself.In other words, India’s cheap labour no longer simply competes with automation. It could also cut the global cost of training robots and large language models. The point to contemplate is not merely whether machines will displace workers. It’s whether the knowledge workers bring becomes a strategic resource whose value is realised elsewhere. History isn’t reassuring here and we know that economies that supplied essential raw materials often had little control over the industries built around them, and their competitiveness suffered. That’s why Frank Herbert’s Dune offers such a valuable metaphor.In Dune, Arrakis, a barren desert planet, possesses spice, the indispensable resource on which an advanced civilisation relies for interstellar travel. However, owning this resource does not automatically mean dominance over the system built around it. Instead, others coordinate its extraction, trade, and conversion into power. India faces a version of that dilemma in the emerging physical AI economy. Its spice is the vast stock of embodied knowledge held by its workers - the accumulated judgement, dexterity, and experience in how tasks are performed. Indian companies can collect and annotate worker data but risk missing out on valuable layers if India remains just a raw knowledge supplier, as key datasets, models, robotics, software, platforms, and machines are mainly owned elsewhere. India is repeating an old development pattern in a new technological form.India’s previous outsourcing boom was built on supplying labour to the West. Physical AI raises the prospect that India will now also supply the knowledge embedded in that labour, captured as data and used to train robots, machines, and large language models worldwide. The strategic challenge for India, then, is to make sure it doesn’t remain merely the source of that input. That means guarding its data privacy and sovereignty, while also developing its own models, robotic capabilities, and intellectual property built on that data.India doesn’t need to stop the flow of spice. It just needs to make sure it doesn’t become merely Arrakis.(Amit Kapoor is chair & Sheen Zutshi isresearch manager atInstitute for Competitiveness.).

articles.title: Domestic aviation industry may post losses of ₹38,000 cr in FY27: Icra
articles.summary:
The Indian aviation industry is expected to post net losses of Rs 36,000-38,000 crore in the current fiscal, compared to estimated net losses of Rs 28,000-30,000 crore in the previous year, ratings agency ICRA said on Thursday.
The losses were primarily driven by moderation in passenger traffic growth, rising aviation turbine fuel (ATF) prices and forex losses arising from the sharp depreciation of the Indian rupee, it said.
The onset of the war in West Asia in late February 2026 is expected to dampen air passenger traffic growth in FY27, ICRA said.
Additionally, increased costs due to depreciation of the Indian Rupee against the US dollar, elevated ATF prices and a rise in lease rentals amid continued aircraft deliveries are projected to cause a net loss of Rs 36,000-38,000 crore in this fiscal.
These cost escalations may not be adequately passed on to passengers through fare hikes, it said.

North Korea fires 10 ballistic missiles towards sea amid border tensions
articles.summary:
North Korea launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward the sea Thursday, South Korea's military said, days after the North threatened to resume front-line propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy new weapons along the rivals' tense border.
The launches also followed leader Kim Jong Un's surprise weekend visit to China, the North's main ally and economic pipeline, to push for greater cooperation.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected about 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the North's eastern costal town of Wonsan. It said South Korea's military bolstered its surveillance posture and was closely exchanging information about the launches with the US and Japan.
Animosity between the Koreas have deepened after last month's land mine blasts that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of planting mines south of the military demarcation line that caused the Sept 21 blasts, but Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions

articles.title: EPFO plans to invest in startups, AIFs
articles.summary: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is working on guidelines to enable investments in alternative investment funds (AIFs), five years after the government cleared the retirement body’s entry into these high-growth asset classes and startups, The Times of India reported on Thursday.The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) discussed a proposal to allocate up to 3% of EPFO’s fresh annual accretions to Category I and Category II AIFs at an investment committee meeting last Thursday, the report said.The move could mark a shift in how the retirement fund body deploys workers’ savings, allowing it to gain exposure to startups and other growth-oriented investments beyond its traditional debt instruments.The proposal will now be placed before the central board of trustees, headed by Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, in November, according to the report.The development follows a September letter from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) seeking EPFO’s participation in the recently launched Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0.The proposal prompted discussions on a broader framework for investments in AIFs, the report added.Initially, EPFO is considering routing investments through institutional entities such as the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and the Small Industries Development Bank of India’s (SIDBI) Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0.Under the investment pattern notified by the finance ministry, EPFO can invest up to 5% of its fresh accretions in asset-backed and trust-structured investments. It has not yet invested in SEBI-regulated Category I and Category II AIFs.Category I AIFs typically support startups, small businesses, infrastructure and venture capital, while Category II funds include private equity, real estate and private debt funds.The proposed framework includes safeguards such as a minimum AIF corpus of Rs 100 crore, limits on exposure to individual funds, restrictions on investments in foreign-incorporated entities and requirements for fund manager independence.EPFO manages around Rs 30 lakh crore in retirement savings for nearly 30 crore members, the report said.
